subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, prove that a cos²(A/2) + b cos²(B/2) + c cos²(C/2) = s + Δ/R.

mark_split.label: Convert the sides by the sine rule

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.47 — LAQ chapter 6 Properties of Triangles, answer 36. Printed appearances: TS 15, plus the pre-bifurcation tag 'IPE 13' which appearances[] cannot carry. The right-hand side has two pieces and the proof produces them separately: the s comes from the constant half of the half-angle expansion, the Δ/R from the rest. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer. recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

steps.label: Expand the half angles
steps.margin_note: Two marks. cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2 splits every term into a plain side and a side-times-cosine — and the plain sides are what become s.
lines: L.H.S = a cos²(A/2) + b cos²(B/2) + c cos²(C/2)
= s + (a cosA + b cosB + c cosC)/2   [∵ (a+b+c)/2 = s]

recall.must_convey: That cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2 is used and the constant part collects to s.
accept: cos squared half A is one plus cos A over two so the plain sides give a plus b plus c over two which is s
split each term and the sides add to s
the s comes from the halves of the sides
cos square half A ni one plus cos A by two ga rasi split cheyyali
expand the half angles and collect the constant part
heard_as: one plus cos A over two
a plus b plus c over two

steps.why: The s on the right-hand side appears immediately and never changes again. Separating it out early leaves only one thing left to prove.
common_mistakes: Using cos²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2, which is the sine form.

steps.label: Convert the sides by the sine rule
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. a = 2R sinA turns each term into 2R sinA cosA, which is R sin2A — bringing double angles in.
lines: a cosA + b cosB + c cosC
= 2R sinA cosA + 2R sinB cosB + 2R sinC cosC   [∵ a = 2R sinA]
= R(2 sinA cosA + 2 sinB cosB + 2 sinC cosC)

recall.must_convey: That a = 2R sinA is used and each term becomes R sin 2A.
accept: use a equals two R sin A so each term becomes two R sin A cos A which is R sin two A
the sine rule turns the sides into sines and the double angle appears
it becomes R times the sum of sin two A sin two B sin two C
a equals two R sin A vaadi sin two A ga marchali
convert the sides using the sine rule

steps.why: The sine rule is the only bridge between sides and angles here. Once every side is a sine, the double-angle formula does the rest.
common_mistakes: Using a = R sinA without the 2.
Forgetting to factor the R out.

steps.label: Use the sin2A identity
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. sin2A + sin2B + sin2C = 4 sinA sinB sinC in any triangle — the Unit 6 identity, quoted here rather than re-proved.
lines: = R(4 sinA sinB sinC)   [∵ in a △, sin2A+sin2B+sin2C = 4 sinA sinB sinC]

recall.must_convey: That sin2A + sin2B + sin2C = 4 sinA sinB sinC is quoted, giving s + 2R sinA sinB sinC.
accept: in a triangle sin two A plus sin two B plus sin two C is four sin A sin B sin C
quote the identity from the transformations chapter
it becomes s plus two R sin A sin B sin C
triangle lo aa identity vaadali, four sin A sin B sin C
use the standard sum identity
heard_as: four sin A sin B sin C

steps.why: This is exactly the identity proved as Unit 6 answer 26.1. Quoting a proved result rather than re-deriving it is what keeps a 7-mark answer inside its time.
common_mistakes: Trying to re-prove the identity and running out of time.
Halving wrongly and losing the factor of 2.

steps.label: Convert to Δ/R
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Multiply and divide by R: 2R² sinA sinB sinC is Δ, so the whole term becomes Δ/R.
lines: = s + (2R² sinA sinB sinC)/R   [multiplying and dividing by R]
= s + Δ/R   [∵ Δ = 2R² sinA sinB sinC]

recall.must_convey: That multiplying and dividing by R gives 2R² sinA sinB sinC = Δ, so the term is Δ/R.
accept: multiply and divide by R so two R squared sin A sin B sin C is delta giving delta over R
use delta equals two R squared sin A sin B sin C
the last term becomes delta over R
R tho multiply and divide cheste delta by R vasthundi
convert the product into delta over R

steps.why: Δ = 2R² sinA sinB sinC is another standard result. Manufacturing the second R is the only way to reach it from 2R sinA sinB sinC.
common_mistakes: Not introducing the second R and being unable to finish.
Writing Δ = R² sinA sinB sinC without the 2.
